results.content:
### What Can We Do About All This

That is about everything we know about the more esoteric aspects of the IBJJF’s seeding and bracketing system. Needless to say, it’s the official stance of Jiujitsu.net that the current system is too convoluted, opaque, and ultimately unfair to the athletes. Instead, we advise the IBJJF do the following:

1. Assign a statistical rating to each athlete; this rating is a single number that follows the athlete across age and belt divisions. Whenever it comes time to rank athletes for seeding purposes, sort the athletes by rating. That’s it. Your rating is your seed, end of story.
2. Switch to using standard “snake” brackets instead of the current ad-hoc bracket layouts. [...] Lavaselli, who medaled at adult Euros and Pans, nevertheless had fewer “Grand Slam” points than his competitors, who placed in similar tournaments in the masters divisions. This is one of the many ways that the IBJJF’s current ranking system produces nonsensical results (unlike ours, which would have seeded Lavaselli first; Lavaselli would go on to win the division in convincing fashion).

That said, there is one element of the “non-transferrable” statement that holds true: points don’t transfer between belts. This is another huge cause of mis-seeding in the IBJJF, where the highest ranked colored belt athletes always “start over” at zero points when they get promoted to the next belt (again, fixed by our system, where your Elo rating follows you through the belts). [...] We saw a fun application of this status when Omar Salum announced he would be competing in the adult division at Worlds 2026 for the first time in over twenty years. The dedicated master 5 competitor with no adult points ended up seeded right in the middle of the light feather pack at 14th out of 26 athletes.

Note that, like all world champions, Salum’s requirement of 80 ranking points is waived for Worlds, along with his entry fee. In fact, the IBJJF also gives no-gi world champions the same benefit, which explains how Tommy Langaker was able to compete at this year’s Worlds, despite not earning a gi medal since 2022. But despite this, no-gi world champions still aren’t “former world champions” in gi division seeding. I guess the IBJJF’s respect for no-gi has its limits.

# About This App

JiuJitsu.net ranks competitors and provides a comprehensive database of matches in events run by the International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation. We are an independant site and are not affiliated with the IBJJF.

Competitors are rated using the Elo rating system, which is a method for calculating the relative skill levels of players in competitive games. We allow users to search for competitors, view their ratings, and see their match history.

This app is a work in progress and is being developed by Dan Lukehart and Will Weisser. The source code is available on GitHub. Ratings may be subject to change as the app is developed and improved. [...] We host and maintain this app as a free service to the jiu-jitsu community. If you would like to support us, please consider donating.

If you would like a copy of our source data for research purposes, contact us and we'll be happy to help. You have permission to use data or screenshots from this site in articles, blog posts, and other media, but we ask that you credit JiuJitsu.net. All other uses of our data, including commercial use, is prohibited without an explicit license.

# Full Disclaimer

While we only rank athletes who compete in the International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation, this site is not affiliated, endorsed by, or associated with the IBJJF. [...] Q: Are you going to track kids divisions?

A: We have decided to store a searchable list of teen matches as some of these athletes are beginning their serious competitive journey in the sport. However, we do not compute ratings for teens and we do not track younger divisions in order to promote a healthy competitive environment for children.

Q: What are the "Elite" badges on some athlete profiles?

A: We assign an "Elite" badge to athletes whose ratings are among the top competitors in the same belt, weight and age divisions (or across all weights in the same age, a.k.a. Pound-for-Pound / P4P). These badges are a mark of achievement and allow fans to easily recognize when an elite athlete is competing and follow their progress.
